1.goal: To open on something she has actually wanted to ask and did not.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class and whether she wrote the six questions.

Say what today is: she asks you six questions now, you write them down, later in the lesson she checks them, and in the final activity she asks questions to find out about you or about an invented person.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “You ask me six questions now, and I write them down. Later in the lesson you look at them again. In the final activity you ask more questions to find out about me or about a new person.”
1.expected: Something she wanted to ask a teacher, a video, a person online. It may come in Portuguese.
1.support: Offer two: something at school, or something outside it.
1.challenge: Ask what stopped her from asking it.
1.monitoring: Whether the thing that stopped her was the words or the order.
1.evidence: What she says stops her asking. It is worth more than any of the six questions.
1.transition: Move on when she knows that the six questions are written down now and checked later in the lesson.

2.goal: To collect six questions of hers, unhelped, as the evidence the whole lesson is measured against.
2.interaction: S–T. She asks, you answer briefly.
run: Ask for the six, following the three lines on screen: two about the weekend, two about work, two about anything.
Write each question down exactly as she says it, including any mistakes in word order.
Answer each question briefly, responding to what she asked, so the exchange works as a real conversation.
Leave the correction for screen 9. If she asks whether a question was right, tell her you are writing it down and that you check the six together on screen 9.
exact: Setting it up: “Ask me six questions about my week. I answer them and write them down.”
If she asks whether it was right: “I am writing it down. We check all six together later in the lesson.”
2.expected: Six questions about your week. Some may have the words in the wrong order; her profile describes this as an occasional problem.
2.support: If she cannot think of one, give her the topic and not the words: “Something about Sunday.”
2.challenge: Ask for a seventh that she would not normally dare to ask.
2.monitoring: Which ones come out scrambled and of what kind: missing auxiliary, double past, or no inversion at all.
2.evidence: The six questions, verbatim. This is the diagnostic of the lesson and the record that matters most.
2.transition: Move on once you have the six questions written down.

3.goal: To meet six real questions in a context where nobody is thinking about grammar.
3.interaction: T–S, reading the exchange out loud together, one line each.
run: Read the exchange out loud with her, alternating: she reads one line, you read the next.
Ask her to find the six questions and read them out loud again, without discussing the form.
Ask the question on screen: which one would she find hardest to say, and why?
3.expected: The six questions: Are you new here? Which subjects did you choose? Why does everyone ask me that? Do you know anyone here? Who sits over there? What deadline? The one she names as hardest is often the one with did.
3.support: If she cannot find all six, tell her how many are in each half of the exchange.
3.challenge: Ask which question in the exchange gets the most useful answer.
3.monitoring: Whether she notices anything about the form on her own. Some students do, here.
3.evidence: Which question she calls the hardest. Compare it with what went wrong on screen 2.
3.transition: Move on when she has found the six questions.

4.goal: To choose the correct question in each pair, before the rule is explained.
run: Read the instruction with her: in each pair, she chooses the correct question.
Let her choose in the three pairs on her own, then press Check.
On each pair, ask what is different between the two questions. The explanation opens under each pair after Check.
Do not state the rule yet. Screen 6 does that, after screen 5.
exact: On each pair: “What is different between these two questions?”
4.expected: Pair 1: “Are you new here?” (not “You are new here?”). Pair 2: “Which subjects did you choose?” (not “Which subjects you chose?”). Pair 3: “Did you choose biology?” (not “Did you chose biology?”).
4.support: Read the statement version out loud right before the pair, for example “You are new here.”, and ask what changes in the question.
4.challenge: Ask her to say the wrong question in each pair and correct it out loud.
4.monitoring: Whether she can hear the difference before she can name it.
4.evidence: Whether she chose “Which subjects you chose?” or “Did you chose biology?”. They are the same kind of error as the ones to look for in her six questions.
4.transition: Move on when the three pairs are checked and discussed.

5.goal: To locate do, did, are and can in each sentence and see that, in a question, they go in front of the subject.
run: Let her place the five sentences on her own, then press Check.
Check them by reading each question out loud together with the matching statement: first the statement, then the question.
5.expected: “Are you new here?” — in front of the subject. “You are new here.” — behind the subject. “Did she hand in the group work?” — in front of the subject. “When do you have a break?” — in front of the subject. “She can help you with the deadline.” — behind the subject.
5.support: Ask her to point at do, did, are or can in the sentence before she chooses.
5.challenge: Ask her to turn one of the two statements into a question out loud.
5.monitoring: Whether she sees the pattern herself. If she says it before screen 6, write down how she said it.
5.evidence: Whether she named the pattern before being shown it.
5.transition: Move on when the five are placed. If she has already said the rule, tell her so on the next screen.

6.goal: To explain how a question is made: be and can go in front of the subject, other verbs use do, does or did, and the main verb stays in its base form.
run: Read the three pairs on screen out loud.
Ask the question on screen: in the third pair, what changed besides the new word?
Open the reveal after she has answered, and read it with her, one part at a time.
For each part, ask her for one more example: a question with be or can, one with do, one with does, one with did.
exact: If she does not see the second change: “Look at the verb. It was ‘chose’. What is it now?”
Asking for examples: “Give me a question with does. Who is it about?”
6.expected: In the third pair, did appears and chose changes to choose. From the reveal: be and can go in front of the subject; other verbs use do (present), does (present with he, she, it) or did (past) in front of the subject; after do, does or did, the main verb is in its base form (Did you go?, not Did you went?).
6.support: Cover the third pair and do the first two only, then uncover it.
6.challenge: Ask her to explain in her own words when she uses does instead of do.
6.monitoring: Whether she chooses between do, does and did correctly in her own examples, and whether she keeps the base form after did.
6.evidence: Her own examples with do, does and did, and whether the verb after did stays in the base form.
6.transition: Move on once the reveal has been read and she has given her examples.

7.goal: To handle the one case where nothing moves, by asking who is doing the action.
run: Read the two lines on screen and ask the question: why does the first one have no do in it?
Let her mark the three questions that need no auxiliary, then press Check.
Give her one test to keep: is the question word the one doing the action?
exact: The test, said once and repeated: “Ask yourself: who is doing it? If it is the question word, nothing moves.”
7.expected: The first line has no do because who is the one who sits. No auxiliary: “Who wants to go first?”, “What happened after that?”, “How many people came?”. With an auxiliary: “Who did she talk to?”, “What did you choose?”, “How many people did you invite?”.
7.support: On each item, ask who did the action, and answer it together before she chooses.
7.challenge: Ask her to make one more pair of her own, one of each kind.
7.monitoring: Whether she uses the test or guesses.
7.evidence: Whether the exception sticks or collapses back into the rule.
7.transition: Move on once the six are done and the test has been said out loud.

8.goal: To rebuild six questions quickly, saying each one out loud before checking it.
8.interaction: S alone, at speed, with you timing loosely.
run: Say the rule of the game: choose, say it out loud, then check. In that order.
Let her go through the six without stopping. Do not comment between items.
At the end, go back only to the ones that were wrong, and ask what moved.
exact: The rule of the game: “Choose, say it out loud, then check. Saying it is the part that makes it stick.”
8.expected: “Where did you go on Saturday?” · “How many hours do you work on a Monday?” · “Who taught you English?” · “Why did you become a teacher?” · “Have you ever lived in another country?” · “What are you doing this weekend?”. “Who taught you English?” is the one without an auxiliary, the same case as screen 7.
8.support: If she is choosing without saying, stop and ask her to say the last one out loud before moving on.
8.challenge: Ask her to say all six again from memory, in order.
8.monitoring: Speed and accuracy together. Getting it right slowly is not the same as having it.
8.evidence: How many were right at speed, and whether she actually said them out loud.
8.transition: Move on when the six are done.

9.goal: To look again at her six questions from screen 2, check which ones have mistakes, and ask those again.
9.interaction: T–S. You read her questions back; she repeats and checks each one.
run: Read her first question back exactly as she said it on screen 2.
Ask her to repeat it and say whether it has any mistakes. Wait for her answer before you comment.
If it has a mistake, ask her to say the question again the way she would say it now. If it was already correct, tell her so and go to the next one.
Do the same with all six.
exact: Reading one back: “You asked me: ‘…’. Repeat it. Does it have any mistakes?”
If it needs correcting: “How would you ask it now?”
9.expected: For each of the six: whether it has a mistake, and, for the ones with mistakes, a new version with the auxiliary in front of the subject and the verb in its base form after do, does or did. The key is your notes from screen 2.
9.support: If she cannot see what to change, ask where do, did, are or can is in her question.
9.challenge: Ask her which of the six she would still not be sure about tomorrow.
9.monitoring: How many mistakes she finds without help, and how many she corrects without help.
9.evidence: Which of the six she corrected on her own, compared with your notes from screen 2.
9.transition: Move on when all six have been checked.

10.goal: To choose who she will ask, option A or option B, and to prepare three questions with the word order from the lesson.
10.interaction: T–S to choose, then S alone, writing.
run: Read the two options with her. In option A she chooses one topic and asks you; in option B she chooses Leo or Sofia and you play that person.
Once she has chosen, give her about four minutes to write three questions. Do not correct what she writes.
Before she starts, tell her that on the next screen she asks the questions without reading them.
exact: Before she starts: “Write three questions. On the next screen you ask them without reading, so write questions you can remember.”
10.expected: Three questions for the topic or person she chose, most of them with do, did, are or can in front of the subject.
10.support: If she cannot start, point to one topic or one line of the profile and ask what she wants to know about it.
10.challenge: Ask her to write one question where the question word is the subject, like “Who taught you English?”.
10.monitoring: Whether the written questions have the words in the right order more often than her six questions from screen 2.
10.evidence: The option she chose and her three written questions.
10.transition: Move on when three questions are written.

11.goal: To ask the prepared questions without reading, and to ask one more question about each answer.
11.interaction: S–T, sustained. She asks; you answer as yourself (option A) or as Leo or Sofia (option B).
run: Ask her to put the paper down before the first question.
If she chose option A, answer as yourself about the topic she chose.
If she chose option B, play the person in the profile and answer freely, in character. You can add details that are not in the profile.
Answer each question briefly, so there is room for one more question about the answer. Do not correct during the conversation; write down word-order mistakes for screen 12.
At the end, ask her to say three things she found out.
exact: Setting it up for option B: “Now I am Leo. Ask me your questions.” (or Sofia)
If she moves on after one answer: “Do you want to know anything else about that?”
11.expected: Three questions and at least one follow-up question built on an answer, then three things she found out.
11.support: If she cannot remember a question, give her the first word only.
11.challenge: Answer one question with something surprising and stop, so she has to ask a follow-up question.
11.monitoring: How many questions came from your answers and not from her paper, and the word order in each question.
11.evidence: The number of follow-up questions, whether she asked without reading, and the word-order mistakes you wrote down.
11.transition: Move on when she has said the three things she found out.

12.goal: To give feedback on the conversation and repeat the task with a person she has not asked yet.
12.interaction: T–S for the feedback, then S–T for the new round.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve.
Write one of her questions from screen 11 and a clearer version of it side by side in the boxes.
Open the replay. She chooses Leo or Sofia, a person she has not asked yet; if she chose option A on screen 10, she can choose either one.
Play that person and answer freely. She asks three questions and one more question about each answer.
exact: Starting the new round: “Choose a person you have not asked yet. I am that person now.”
12.expected: Three questions to the new person, with follow-up questions, and the point to improve used at least once.
12.support: If she stops, point to one line of the profile and wait.
12.challenge: Answer each question with one short sentence only, so she has to ask more.
12.monitoring: Whether the point to improve from the feedback boards appears in the new round.
12.evidence: Whether the point to improve changed in the second round.
12.transition: Move on to the close when the new round is over.

13.goal: To close the lesson with what was worked on and where it goes.
13.interaction: T–S, ticking the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Say the homework out loud: this week, ask one more question about the answer, instead of moving on.
exact: The homework: “This week, when someone answers you, ask one more thing about the answer. One. That is all.”
13.expected: Her own reading of the lesson. The question about which answer was most interesting usually gets a real answer.
13.support: If the confidence is low, go back to the questions she corrected herself on screen 9.
13.challenge: Ask what surprised her in the answers she got on screens 11 and 12.
13.monitoring: Whether she leaves thinking of questions as something she can do rather than something she gets wrong.
13.evidence: Her confidence marks, and what she said about the pre-class.
13.transition: End here. The next lesson is the one that closes the block: two minutes about her, and what she wants to do.
